output.impression: 1. No traumatic cord lesion, fracture, ligamentous injury or epidural haematoma. 2. Mild smooth enhancement of the cauda equina nerve roots, which can be seen in an inflammatory polyradiculopathy.

output.interpretation: Hospital day 2. Opening pressure 156 mmH2O (normal). Faint xanthochromia and RBC 450/mm3, indicating subarachnoid blood. WBC 8/mm3, predominantly lymphocytes. Protein 92 mg/dL (elevated); at about 1 mg/dL of protein per 1000 RBC/mm3, the red cells account for under 1 mg/dL of the protein. Glucose 58 mg/dL (CSF:serum ratio 0.68). Gram stain no organisms; culture no growth; HSV PCR not detected. Elevated protein with a mildly raised cell count. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings: Non-invasive blood pressure 132/70 to 182/98 mmHg, with swings of 40 mmHg systolic within an hour
output.impression: 24-hour continuous telemetry (hospital days 1-2). Sinus tachycardia 96-124 bpm. No pauses, bradyarrhythmia or atrial arrhythmia. Labile blood pressure, 132/70 to 182/98 mmHg.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC in L, % predicted and mL/kg, MIP and MEP, with the trend; ICU-level monitoring if FVC <20 mL/kg or <60% predicted, MIP weaker than -30 cmH2O, MEP <40 cmH2O, a fall of more than 30%, or bulbar weakness with weak cough
action_criteria.label: Bedside respiratory function (FVC, MIP, MEP), repeated serially while weakness progresses
action_criteria.rationale: He is deteriorating with bulbar weakness, a weak cough and SpO2 93%; bedside FVC, MIP and MEP, interpreted with the clinical signs, decide intubation now [Lawn_2001, EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No cord contusion, compression, fracture or epidural haematoma; nerve root enhancement may be seen
action_criteria.label: Contrast MRI of the whole spine to exclude a traumatic cord or spinal lesion
action_criteria.rationale: New flaccid quadriparesis after a fall must be imaged for a cervical cord injury before it is attributed to GBS; bulbar weakness and a delayed onset argue against a cord lesion but do not replace imaging [EAN_PNS_2023, Leonhard_2019].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Polyradiculoneuropathy pattern (demyelinating or axonal features, absent F-waves, sural sparing where present); may be normal in the first week
action_criteria.label: Nerve conduction studies and needle EMG
action_criteria.rationale: Nerve conduction studies show the demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy that separates GBS from cord injury, critical illness neuropathy and myopathy; early studies can be abnormal in F-waves and distal latencies first [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Raised protein (92 mg/dL) not explained by the 450 RBC/mm3; 8 cells/mm3 is compatible with GBS but prompts exclusion of infection (Gram stain and culture negative); >50/mm3 would suggest another diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Lumbar puncture for CSF cell count, protein and glucose
action_criteria.rationale: CSF supports the diagnosis; here it must be read against the subarachnoid blood: 450 RBC/mm3 add under 1 mg/dL of protein, so the raised protein is not explained by the haemorrhage, and 8 cells/mm3 is compatible but prompts exclusion of infection [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Baseline values before treatment, with normal platelets and coagulation; normal potassium; CK falling after the crush injury; abnormal liver tests or low albumin mark a higher risk of a severe course
action_criteria.label: Baseline blood tests: full blood count, renal function and electrolytes, liver tests, albumin, glucose, CK and coagulation
action_criteria.rationale: Baseline blood tests, including the platelet count and coagulation before the lumbar puncture in a patient with traumatic intracranial haemorrhage taking aspirin; potassium excludes a hypokalaemic paralysis and CK tracks the crush injury [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Continuous telemetry with blood pressure monitoring: sinus tachycardia 96-124 bpm and labile blood pressure 132/70 to 182/98 mmHg in the first 24 hours; autonomic instability (rate and blood pressure lability, bradyarrhythmia) requires continued monitoring while weakness progresses
action_criteria.label: Continuous inpatient cardiac telemetry with blood pressure monitoring while weakness progresses
action_criteria.rationale: Autonomic dysfunction is common in GBS and can cause bradyarrhythmias, pauses and blood-pressure lability; monitoring continues while weakness progresses [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus tachycardia, rate 106, with a prolonged QTc of 462 ms
action_criteria.label: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to screen for autonomic dysrhythmias and baseline QTc
action_criteria.rationale: A baseline 12-lead ECG screens for autonomic rhythm and conduction changes and gives the QTc before treatment [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Donepezil prolongs succinylcholine block and adds vagotonic and QT effects to autonomic instability; aspirin matters with traumatic intracranial haemorrhage and central line placement
action_criteria.label: Check the medication list for interactions with donepezil and aspirin before intubation, LP and IVIg or plasma exchange
action_criteria.rationale: Donepezil changes the choice of neuromuscular blocker and adds to bradyarrhythmia and QT risk with a QTc of 462 ms; aspirin bears on the haemorrhage and on procedures (ROUND_POLICY ruling 6).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on immunotherapy in GBS; not needed for the diagnosis or the treatment decision
action_criteria.label: Optional literature search on IVIg versus plasma exchange in GBS
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step of the work-up.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat with corticosteroids: oral corticosteroids are strongly advised against and IV methylprednisolone is not recommended [EAN_PNS_2023].
Do not start IVIg without checking renal function.
Do not use succinylcholine for intubation.
required_recommendations: Intubate electively now in the ICU: FVC 1.3 L (16 mL/kg, below 20 mL/kg), MIP -22 cmH2O and MEP 30 cmH2O, with bulbar weakness, a weak cough, aspiration of thin liquids and SpO2 93% on room air, while weakness is still progressing [EAN_PNS_2023, Lawn_2001].
Avoid succinylcholine for intubation (risk of hyperkalaemia after denervation, and prolonged block with donepezil); use a non-depolarising agent.

Start IVIg 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total, about 32 g/day at 80 kg) now; plasma exchange (200-250 mL/kg over 5 sessions) is an equivalent alternative, with relative caution for haemodynamic instability and central venous access [EAN_PNS_2023].
Continuous cardiac telemetry with blood pressure monitoring in the ICU while weakness progresses; hold donepezil while bradyarrhythmia risk is high (vagotonic effect, QTc 462 ms).
Hold aspirin while there is traumatic intracranial haemorrhage, and agree with neurosurgery when it restarts.
Thromboprophylaxis with intermittent pneumatic compression now, and low-molecular-weight heparin once neurosurgery confirms the haemorrhage is stable [Leonhard_2019].

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Brain MRI was done on admission; a repeat adds nothing to a lower motor neuron, areflexic quadriparesis with bulbar weakness and unchanged consciousness.

accepted: Severe Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy) after head trauma

differential.diagnosis: Traumatic cervical cord injury (including spinal shock)
differential.key_features: Areflexic quadriparesis after a fall raises it, but he moved all limbs on day 1, the weakness ascended over hours, bulbar muscles are involved, and MRI shows no cord lesion, fracture or ligamentous injury.
Onset on hospital day 2, before the 1-2 weeks of critical illness these need, with no sepsis or multiorgan failure, and a demyelinating rather than axonal NCS.
CK 20,518 falling to 9,640 U/L, but muscle injury does not cause areflexia, bulbar weakness or a demyelinating NCS.
Low-grade fever and leukocytosis after trauma, but no infective source on examination, blood cultures without growth at 48 h, and CSF Gram stain and culture negative with 8 lymphocytic cells.
The PRES-like lesions and the thin subdural do not produce flaccid areflexic quadriparesis with bulbar weakness and unchanged consciousness.
Cannot be excluded at presentation; progression beyond 8 weeks or 3 or more treatment-related fluctuations would point to it. Reassess at 8 weeks.

key_clinical_evidence: Rapidly ascending flaccid quadriparesis with bulbar weakness and global areflexia, raised CSF protein and a demyelinating NCS: Brighton level 1 once the course plateaus within 4 weeks (CSF cells under 50 with raised protein, NCS consistent) [Brighton_2011].
Blood in the CSF raises protein by only about 1 mg/dL per 1000 RBC/mm3; with 450 RBC/mm3 the protein of 92 mg/dL is not explained by the subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Critical illness polyneuropathy and myopathy need 1-2 weeks of critical illness; weakness on hospital day 2 with a demyelinating NCS is not CIP.
Onset 2 days after the fall is shorter than the usual interval after an antecedent event; the diagnosis rests on the clinical, CSF and NCS findings, not on a trigger.
Anti-ganglioside antibodies are not needed to diagnose typical GBS; anti-GQ1b is tested when Miller Fisher syndrome or an overlap is suspected [EAN_PNS_2023].
FVC below 20 mL/kg with bulbar weakness, weak cough and falling saturation calls for elective intubation now; the decision combines the numbers with the clinical signs [Lawn_2001, EAN_PNS_2023].

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Spine MRI shows no cord lesion; flaccid areflexic quadriparesis with bulbar weakness, raised CSF protein and a demyelinating NCS is a polyradiculoneuropathy.
red_herrings.data_point: Recent head trauma with subarachnoid haemorrhage and subdural haematoma
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors on cervical cord injury, a central complication or post-traumatic critical illness rather than GBS.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Expected after trauma with crush injury; no infective source, blood cultures without growth, CSF Gram stain and culture negative.
red_herrings.data_point: Low-grade fever (37.9 C) with WBC 19.2 and neutrophils 15.4
red_herrings.intended_effect: Fever at onset counts against GBS and suggests sepsis-related weakness or meningitis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The lesions predate the weakness and do not produce lower motor neuron, areflexic quadriparesis with bulbar weakness.
red_herrings.data_point: Bilateral parieto-occipital lesions on the admission MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a central cause of the new weakness.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Weakness began 2 days after the injection, too early for a vaccine-induced immune response.

sequence_constraints.reason: Platelet count and coagulation are checked before the lumbar puncture in a patient with traumatic intracranial haemorrhage taking aspirin.
Renal function, potassium and the blood count are reviewed with the medication list before intubation drugs and IVIg or plasma exchange are chosen.

interactions: Donepezil and succinylcholine: cholinesterase inhibitors exaggerate and prolong depolarising neuromuscular blockade (product labelling).
Donepezil: vagotonic effects (sinus bradycardia, heart block) and reported QT prolongation; additive with other bradycardic or QT-prolonging drugs (product labelling).

Aspirin: antiplatelet effect lasts the life of the platelet; relevant to traumatic intracranial haemorrhage and to central venous access for plasma exchange. Aspirin alone is not regarded as a contraindication to lumbar puncture.
Amlodipine: additive hypotension with sedative and induction agents.
general.proposed: Rapid-sequence intubation, IVIg or plasma exchange, lumbar puncture; current medicines donepezil, amlodipine, aspirin
general.summary: Category-level findings: donepezil potentiates succinylcholine and has vagotonic and QT effects; aspirin carries antiplatelet risk with intracranial haemorrhage and line placement; amlodipine adds to hypotension at induction.
warnings: No pharmacokinetic interaction identified between IVIg and donepezil, amlodipine or aspirin.

ecg.interpretation: Sinus tachycardia, rate 106. Normal PR and QRS intervals. Prolonged QTc (462 ms). No acute ST-T changes.

labs.interpretation: Hospital day 2. Leukocytosis (WBC 19.2) with neutrophilia (15.4). AST 96 U/L (elevated). CK 9,640 U/L (elevated). CRP 13.4 mg/L (elevated). Remaining values within reference ranges.

results.finding: Guidelines for adults with GBS who cannot walk unaided advise IVIg 2 g/kg over 5 days within 2 weeks of onset or plasma exchange within 4 weeks, with no preference between them; corticosteroids are not advised.
A second IVIg course in patients with a poor predicted prognosis did not improve outcome and caused more serious adverse events.

general.summary: IVIg or plasma exchange is advised for adults with GBS unable to walk unaided; neither is preferred, and a second IVIg course is not advised [EAN_PNS_2023, Walgaard_2021].

findings.finding: DML 6.4 ms (prolonged; normal <4.4); CV 41 m/s (reduced; normal >49); CMAP 3.2 mV (reduced; normal >4.0)
DML 7.8 ms (prolonged; normal <6.0); CV 34 m/s (reduced; normal >41); CMAP 1.6 mV (reduced; normal >2.0)
Tibialis anterior and first dorsal interosseous: reduced recruitment of normal-morphology motor units; no fibrillation potentials or positive sharp waves

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL study (bedside, hospital day 2). 1. Prolonged distal motor latencies, reduced conduction velocities and reduced CMAP amplitudes in median and peroneal motor nerves. 2. Absent F-waves in all tested nerves; absent H-reflexes. 3. Reduced median with normal sural sensory amplitudes. 4. Reduced recruitment without denervation on needle EMG. Findings are consistent with an acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

metadata.difficulty_description: GBS on hospital day 2 after head trauma with SAH: cord injury, critical illness neuropathy, sepsis and rhabdomyolysis must be separated, the CSF read against subarachnoid blood, and intubation decided now.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 6 required actions (respiratory function, NCS/EMG, CSF, baseline labs with coagulation, telemetry, interaction check for donepezil and aspirin) plus recommended spine MRI; 4 red herrings (trauma, fever with leukocytosis, PRES-like lesions, tetanus toxoid).
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 GBS audit: spine MRI is optional and limited to five cases with a concrete cord, traumatic, postoperative or infiltrative alternative; generic hidden MRI reports removed.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive ascending weakness of all four limbs with bulbar weakness on hospital day 2 after admission for head trauma with subarachnoid haemorrhage.

past_medical_history: Fall while hiking 2 days ago with head injury and multiple bruises; admitted (see history of present illness)

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. W. is a 72-year-old man with vascular dementia who was admitted 2 days ago after a fall while hiking, with a head injury and multiple bruises. On admission (hospital day 0) his GCS was 13. CT head showed a small-volume traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage, a thin convexity subdural haematoma without mass effect or midline shift, and bilateral parieto-occipital hypodensities; CT angiography showed no aneurysm. MRI brain the same day showed bilateral parieto-occipital T2/FLAIR hyperintensities without restricted diffusion, reported as consistent with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome; MR angiography was normal. CK was 20,518 U/L, attributed to crush injury of the thighs. He received tetanus toxoid, his abrasions were dressed, and blood cultures drawn for a temperature of 38.0 C show no growth at 48 hours. He was moving all four limbs and walking with assistance on hospital day 1. Since this morning (hospital day 2) he has developed progressive ascending weakness of all four limbs: he can no longer lift his legs from the bed and his arms are markedly weak. He has a weak voice, a reduced gag and coughs on sips of water. He is still worsening, and his SpO2 has fallen to 93% on room air. There is no new headache or vomiting, and his level of consciousness is unchanged from admission.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Day 2: mild dysarthria with a weak voice; gag reduced bilaterally; coughs on sips of water. Pupils equal and reactive; eye movements full to command.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Day 2: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), unchanged from admission. Confused, limited historian; known baseline vascular dementia. Obeys simple commands.
neurological_exam.motor: Day 2: flaccid weakness of all four limbs. Hip flexion 2/5, knee extension 2/5, ankle dorsiflexion 1/5 bilaterally. Shoulder abduction 3/5, grip 3+/5 bilaterally. Neck flexion 3/5. Cannot lift his legs from the bed.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Day 2: absent throughout (biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, knee and ankle) bilaterally. Plantar responses mute.
neurological_exam.sensory: Day 2: limited by confusion; appears reduced to pinprick and vibration distally in the legs. No sensory level elicited.

physical_exam.general: Weight 80 kg, height 175 cm. Bruising over both thighs and the left flank; scalp laceration healing. Chest clear on auscultation; no wound erythema or discharge.
